claims.text: Dynamic mechanical behavior in solidified, Co-free equiatomic FeNiCrMn is governed by a transition among discontinuous dynamic recrystallization, dislocation slip, and mechanical twinning.
Higher temperature and lower strain rate activate discontinuous dynamic recrystallization.
Discontinuous dynamic recrystallization causes significant grain refinement.
Grain refinement produced by discontinuous dynamic recrystallization enhances ductility.
Lower temperature and higher strain rate limit discontinuous dynamic recrystallization.
When discontinuous dynamic recrystallization is limited, FeNiCrMn deforms predominantly through dislocation slip and mechanical twinning.
Dislocation slip and mechanical twinning under low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading preserve higher strength.
Temperature and strain rate modulate the activation energy for discontinuous dynamic recrystallization.
Increased grain-boundary mobility at high temperature and low strain rate promotes discontinuous dynamic recrystallization.
High-temperature, low-strain-rate specimens will have a high fraction of recrystallized grains and a refined grain structure.
High-temperature, low-strain-rate specimens will exhibit improved ductility.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate specimens will retain relatively coarse grains and develop a higher density of mechanical twins.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate specimens will exhibit increased flow strength.
Prior high-entropy-alloy studies demonstrate discontinuous dynamic recrystallization effects during thermomechanical processing.
The relevant prior benchmarks are comparable-performance equiatomic alloys, including Co-containing alloys.
Direct evidence that discontinuous dynamic recrystallization controls dynamic behavior in Co-free FeNiCrMn is limited.
The proposed material is equiatomic, Co-free FeNiCrMn in an as-solidified, homogenized state with minimal pre-existing defects.
The proposed comparison uses 800 K at 0.001 s^-1 versus room temperature at 0.1 s^-1 and measures microstructure by EBSD and TEM alongside stress-strain behavior.
